title: Beyond Memory: Harnessing Long-Horizon Agents with Explicit Belief States

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
LLM agents are increasingly equipped with ultra-long context windows ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2026a ; Hu et al., 2026 ) , stronger reasoning and tool-use capabilities ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Feng et al., 2026 ) , external memory systems ( Hu et al., 2025 ; Kang et al., 2025 ; Wei et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026b ) , and sophisticated execution harnesses ( Ma et al., 2026 ; Wan et al., 2026 ) , substantially expanding the complexity and horizon of tasks they can undertake.
However, longer interaction horizons expose a deeper challenge, as actions may alter the environment and new observations may invalidate earlier inferences.
Accumulated context thus mixes evidence about past states with intermediate judgments, making it increasingly difficult to identify which facts still hold, which inferences remain supported, and what remains unresolved.
Raw trajectories preserve this evidence chronologically, while memory mechanisms select, compress, or reorganize it.
While both are valuable, access to evidence alone does not ensure an explicit and coherent estimate of the current world that can be revised and checked across steps.
Recent work observes that when task state remains implicit within a growing context, outdated or inconsistent information can persist across subsequent decisions ( Ma et al., 2026 ) .
The next barrier to reliable long-horizon LLM agents is therefore not simply retaining more history, but maintaining an actionable representation of the current world.
A formal basis for this representation is the belief state b t ​ ( s ) = P ⁡ ( s t = s ∣ h t ) b_{t}(s)=P(s_{t}=s\mid h_{t}) , the posterior over the current latent world state s t s_{t} given interaction history h t h_{t} .
In a standard partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), this belief is a sufficient statistic for decision-making and can be recursively updated after each action and observation ( Kaelbling et al., 1998 ) .
Recent methods have begun to explicitly represent the belief state through goal-relative reflection, probabilistic hypotheses, structured graphs, or audited task records ( Kim et al., 2025 ; Tang et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2026 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) .
Such representations make the agent’s current understanding of the world available for inspection and revision.
However, explicit belief construction is just the start, as an LLM-generated belief must satisfy two further requirements.
First, belief updates must remain internally consistent and supported by interaction evidence.
Since these updates are generated by the LLM itself, they may introduce conflicting states or unsupported inferences that undermine subsequent decisions and ultimately lead to task failure.
For instance, recording a microwave as both open and closed makes it unclear whether the robot should open it before placing a mug inside.
Continual validation is thus essential to sustain the coherence and evidential support of the evolving belief state.
Second, consistency alone does not prevent the failure mode we term Belief Trapping , where the agent continues to act without making meaningful progress toward the goal.
For example, the agent may repeat ineffective actions, cycle through previously visited states, or gather information that does not help complete the task.
Unproductive interactions will exhaust the available budget before achieving the goal, making timely detection and recovery necessary to restore meaningful task progress.
T 3 detects belief deviation and truncates uninformative trajectories for reinforcement learning, but does not provide a recovery strategy within the ongoing episode ( Zou et al., 2026 ) .
To our knowledge, no existing framework maintains a belief state with both continual consistency validation and online diagnosis and recovery from Belief Trapping .
We introduce P rogression o f S tates ( PoS ), a unified framework that integrates explicit belief modeling, consistency validation, and trapping-aware recovery for long-horizon agent decision-making.
As illustrated in Figure 2 , PoS continually updates a world state of task-relevant Entities, States, and Relations, along with epistemic and achievement gaps that specify what the agent still needs to learn or accomplish.
The agent selects actions from the current belief, while a Belief Sentinel validates updates for internal consistency and support from interaction evidence. PoS also assesses whether belief evolution supports continued task progress using three measures: gap persistence, progress stagnation, and belief recurrence.
It then performs factorized trapping diagnosis along two dimensions, agent dynamics and blocked gap type, and composes corresponding recovery constraints to recover from Belief Trapping .
We evaluate PoS using three LLM backbones on ALFWorld and LOCA-Bench for execution tasks and RCA-100 and ClinDiag for diagnosis tasks. PoS achieves the highest overall performance on all four benchmarks with each backbone, with relative gains over the strongest baseline reaching 22.68 % 22.68\% on ALFWorld and 37.89 % 37.89\% on RCA-100 joint accuracy.
Ablation studies demonstrate the importance of consistency validation and trapping recovery beyond explicit belief construction.
Further analyses examine trapping patterns and recovery effectiveness, robustness to context growth, and the tradeoff between token consumption and task performance.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: We organize prior approaches to long-horizon context management according to the decision context they expose to the agent: memory as context and belief as context .

sections.heading: 2.1 Memory as Context
sections.text:
ReAct ( Yao et al., 2023 ) provides a foundational framework for LLM agents, conditioning each action on the growing raw interaction trajectory.
Compression-based methods instead summarize accumulated context into compact forms: ReadAgent ( Lee et al., 2024 ) constructs retrievable gist memories, ACON ( Kang et al., 2025 ) optimizes guidelines for history compression, and SUPO ( Lu et al., 2026 ) jointly learns periodic summarization and tool-use policies.
Other methods impose structure on the retained context: HiAgent ( Hu et al., 2025 ) organizes working memory around subgoals, COMPASS ( Wan et al., 2026 ) maintains concise progress briefs across reasoning stages, and PACE ( Wei et al., 2026 ) adjusts historical granularity according to its predicted relevance to the next action.
Other approaches make context management itself an agent-controlled operation: MemGPT manages information across in-context and external memory through an operating-system-inspired hierarchy ( Packer et al., 2023 ) . CaT ( Liu et al., 2026 ) exposes context compression as a callable tool over a structured workspace, AgentFold ( Ye et al., 2026 ) performs proactive multi-scale folding of historical trajectories, and Sculptor ( Li et al., 2026 ) provides explicit tools for actively curating the working context.
Although these methods improve evidence accessibility and context efficiency, the resulting context remains a transformed record of historical evidence rather than a consistent estimate of the current world.

sections.heading: 2.2 Belief as Context
sections.text:
A parallel line of work studies how LLMs represent the current state of an evolving world ( Gurnee and Tegmark, 2024 ) .
Mechanistic studies probe the world-state abstractions encoded by LLMs ( Li et al., 2024 ) and show that state tracking of reasoning is itself a learned computation whose underlying mechanism affects systematic generalization ( Li et al., 2025 ) .
Agent frameworks further externalize parts of this computation ( Tang et al., 2024 ) .
QuBE ( Kim et al., 2024 ) constructs a task-relevant belief through question answering; StateAct ( Rozanov and Rei, 2025 ) maintains a chain of states throughout task execution; and ReflAct ( Kim et al., 2025 ) grounds action selection in reflection over the current state relative to the goal.
More structured approaches maintain particle beliefs over latent states and goals through hypothesis trees and Bayesian filtering ( Tang et al., 2026 ) , recursively update natural-language belief summaries ( Lidayan et al., 2025 ) , or combine causal graphs with state machines as explicit belief ( Luo et al., 2026 ) .
LongHorizon-Harness ( Ma et al., 2026 ) externalizes task state as audited records of requirements, artifacts, and facts, preserving verified progress through a Manage-Execute-Audit loop.
However, it relies on independently verifiable intermediate results and is therefore less suitable when meaningful progress consists of uncertain inferences rather than observable outcomes.
Beyond belief construction, recent work has also begun to address failure modes related to Belief Trapping .
T 3 ( Zou et al., 2026 ) detects excessive belief deviation and truncates uninformative trajectories during reinforcement learning, while CGDP ( Kausik et al., 2026 ) uses an exhaustion gate to terminate unproductive context gathering.
These approaches address stalled progress through truncation or termination, without attempting to restore progress during inference.
In contrast, PoS maintains and validates a task-conditioned belief and uses factorized recovery to redirect subsequent actions.

sections.heading: 3 Methodology
sections.text: PoS comprises three components: Belief Modeling constructs a task-conditioned belief (Section 3.1 ), Belief-Guided Interaction selects actions and validates belief updates (Section 3.2 ), and Trapping-Aware Recovery detects and recovers from Belief Trapping (Section 3.3 ).

sections.heading: 3.1 Belief Modeling
sections.text:
The interaction between a long-horizon agent and its environment can be formulated as a POMDP.
At step t t , the environment has a latent world state s t s_{t} that is not directly observable.
Given the interaction history h t h_{t} , the belief state b t ​ ( s ) b_{t}(s) represents the posterior distribution over s t s_{t} and provides the basis for selecting an action a t a_{t} .
Following this formulation, PoS maintains a structured, task-conditioned belief B t B_{t} as the agent’s explicit decision context: B t = ( W t , G , Δ t E , Δ t A ) , B_{t}=\left(W_{t},G,\Delta_{t}^{E},\Delta_{t}^{A}\right), (1) where W t W_{t} is a structured estimate of the task-relevant world state, G G specifies the task objective, and Δ t E \Delta_{t}^{E} and Δ t A \Delta_{t}^{A} capture unresolved epistemic and achievement gaps, respectively.

sections.heading: World state ( W t W_{t} ).
sections.text:
Prior work often represents an environment through entities and their relations ( Anokhin et al., 2025 ; Gu et al., 2024 ) .
For long-horizon decision making, however, entity identity and connectivity alone are insufficient: an entity’s condition may change over time, directly affecting which actions are feasible and whether the task goal is satisfied. PoS therefore represents W t W_{t} with an Entity–State–Relation structure that applies across domains and makes such changes explicit.
Within this structure, an Entity denotes an object or agent involved in the task, while a State describes the agent’s current understanding of that Entity in natural language.
A directed Relation captures how Entities and States are connected, including relations between two Entities, two States, or an Entity and a State.
Each State and Relation is annotated with its provenance and confidence, together with supporting evidence when available.
The natural-language descriptions in W t W_{t} provide the flexibility to express domain-specific semantics, while the explicit structure supports consistent belief updates and validation.
Rather than attempting to model the environment exhaustively, W t W_{t} retains only records that can affect action feasibility, outcome assessment, or satisfaction of G G .

sections.heading: Goal-conditioned components ( G G , Δ t E \Delta_{t}^{E} , and Δ t A \Delta_{t}^{A} ).
sections.text:
Although W t W_{t} captures the task-relevant world state, it does not by itself indicate what remains unresolved for completing the task. PoS evaluates W t W_{t} against the task objective and completion criteria specified by G G and represents the unresolved requirements as two complementary gap sets.
Epistemic gaps Δ t E \Delta_{t}^{E} capture information that remains unknown or insufficiently supported, whereas achievement gaps Δ t A \Delta_{t}^{A} capture discrepancies between the current belief and the desired goal state that must be resolved through action.
This distinction separates what the agent still needs to learn from what it still needs to accomplish.
Together, W t W_{t} , G G , Δ t E \Delta_{t}^{E} , and Δ t A \Delta_{t}^{A} allow B t B_{t} to represent both the agent’s current understanding of the world and the remaining requirements for goal completion, making it an actionable decision state.

sections.heading: 3.2 Belief-Guided Interaction
sections.text:
Although B t B_{t} represents both the current world and the unresolved task requirements, it may contain multiple epistemic and achievement gaps.
Giving equal priority to all gaps in Δ t E ∪ Δ t A \Delta_{t}^{E}\cup\Delta_{t}^{A} leaves the agent without a clear focus and may cause it to shift between gaps without making sustained progress on any of them. PoS therefore retains B t B_{t} as the complete decision state while selecting an active gap Δ t ∈ Δ t E ∪ Δ t A \Delta_{t}\in\Delta_{t}^{E}\cup\Delta_{t}^{A} that are the most valuable to address given the current world state and task objective.
The active gap establishes the current focus without discarding the broader world understanding and task context represented by B t B_{t} .
We then formulate action selection as: a t ∼ π ( ⋅ ∣ B t , Δ t , 𝒞 t ) . a_{t}\sim\pi\left(\cdot\mid B_{t},\Delta_{t},\mathcal{C}_{t}\right). (2) Here, 𝒞 t \mathcal{C}_{t} denotes the recovery constraint introduced in Section 3.3 .
It is empty during normal interaction and is applied only when Belief Trapping is detected, as an additional constraint on action selection.
After executing a t a_{t} , the task agent receives the resulting observation o t + 1 o_{t+1} from the environment.
The new observation o t + 1 o_{t+1} provides evidence to update the belief.
The task agent incorporates this evidence into B t B_{t} to form an unverified candidate B ~ t + 1 \widetilde{B}_{t+1} , which cannot yet be committed as B t + 1 B_{t+1} .
Because B ~ t + 1 \widetilde{B}_{t+1} is produced by the task agent itself, it may inherit the agent’s erroneous assumptions, reasoning errors, or hallucinations.
Such errors can produce two forms of inconsistency: internal and external.
Internal inconsistency arises when B ~ t + 1 \widetilde{B}_{t+1} contains mutually conflicting content, such as incompatible States assigned to the same Entity.
External inconsistency arises when B ~ t + 1 \widetilde{B}_{t+1} contradicts the latest observation or other available interaction evidence. PoS therefore introduces the Belief Sentinel to validate B ~ t + 1 \widetilde{B}_{t+1} .
It audits newly added or modified Entities, States, Relations, and Gaps, and returns potential consistency issues to the task agent.
The task agent evaluates this feedback against the available interaction evidence and revises B ~ t + 1 \widetilde{B}_{t+1} before committing the resulting belief as B t + 1 B_{t+1} .
The complete belief update is expressed as B ~ t + 1 = 𝒰 ⁡ ( B t , a t , o t + 1 ) → Belief Sentinel B t + 1 , \widetilde{B}_{t+1}=\mathcal{U}\left(B_{t},a_{t},o_{t+1}\right)\;\xrightarrow{\;\text{\emph{Belief Sentinel}}\;}\;B_{t+1}, (3) where 𝒰 \mathcal{U} denotes the candidate belief update performed by the task agent, and the arrow represents Belief Sentinel validation followed by evidence-based revision by the task agent.
The resulting B t + 1 B_{t+1} serves as the decision state for the next step and the basis for belief health estimation in Section 3.3 , helping reduce the risk that erroneous belief updates are mistaken for actual interaction dynamics.

sections.heading: 3.3 Trapping-Aware Recovery
sections.text:
To assess task progress, PoS tracks changes in the world state and unresolved requirements across successive validated belief transitions.
When Belief Trapping is detected, it performs factorized diagnosis of the trapping dynamics and blocked gap type, then composes corresponding recovery constraints to guide subsequent action selection.

sections.heading: Factorized trapping diagnosis.
sections.text:
Once Belief Trapping is detected, PoS examines validated belief transitions within the same window 𝒲 t \mathcal{W}_{t} to diagnose it along two complementary dimensions: the agent dynamics pattern and the blocked gap type.
First, it classifies the agent dynamics as: ρ t = { Static , d W ​ ( W t , W t − 1 ) ≤ ϵ W , Cycle , R t ≥ θ R ∧ k t ∗ > 1 , Drift , d W ​ ( W t Δ , W t − 1 Δ ) ≤ ϵ W , \rho_{t}=\begin{cases}\mathrm{Static},&d_{W}\!\left(W_{t},W_{t-1}\right)\leq\epsilon_{W},\\
\mathrm{Cycle},&R_{t}\geq\theta_{R}\;\land\;k_{t}^{*}>1,\\
\mathrm{Drift},&d_{W}\!\left(W_{t}^{\Delta},W_{t-1}^{\Delta}\right)\leq\epsilon_{W},\end{cases} (6) where the conditions are evaluated in order, k t ∗ k_{t}^{*} denotes the dominant recurrence lag underlying R t R_{t} , and θ R \theta_{R} is the recurrence threshold for identifying periodic behavior.
Under this hierarchy, Static \mathrm{Static} indicates that the world state remains locally unchanged.
Among non-static cases, Cycle \mathrm{Cycle} captures periodic recurrence, whereas Drift \mathrm{Drift} captures changes in the world state that do not advance its active-gap projection.
Second, PoS identifies the blocked gap type by comparing P E P_{E} and P A P_{A} among nonempty gap sets.
The type with higher persistence is selected: X = E X=E indicates blocked epistemic progress, whereas X = A X=A indicates blocked achievement progress.
Together, the agent dynamics pattern specifies how to escape the current trapping state, while the blocked gap type specifies what progress recovery should restore.

sections.heading: Recovery constraints.
sections.text:
Based on the diagnosed dynamics pattern and blocked gap type, PoS combines a pattern-specific escape constraint with a gap-specific progress constraint: 𝒞 t = 𝒞 pattern ​ ( ρ t , 𝒲 t ) ∪ 𝒞 gap ​ ( X , B t , Δ t ) . \mathcal{C}_{t}=\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{pattern}}\left(\rho_{t},\mathcal{W}_{t}\right)\cup\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{gap}}\left(X,B_{t},\Delta_{t}\right). (7) For Static \mathrm{Static} , the pattern constraint suppresses the ineffective state–action transition.
For Cycle \mathrm{Cycle} , it breaks a recurrent transition identified by k t ∗ k_{t}^{*} .
For Drift \mathrm{Drift} , it re-anchors action selection to the active gap.
The gap-specific constraint instead requires new discriminative evidence when X = E X=E and a task-relevant state change when X = A X=A .
During recovery, the active gap Δ t \Delta_{t} remains unchanged, while 𝒞 t \mathcal{C}_{t} is applied as an additional constraint in Eq. 2 .
After the resulting transition is validated, PoS recomputes ℋ t \mathcal{H}_{t} .
The recovery constraints are released when ℋ t > θ H \mathcal{H}_{t}>\theta_{H} ; otherwise, PoS updates the diagnosis and corresponding constraints.

sections.heading: Benchmarks.
sections.text:
We evaluate PoS on four long-horizon benchmarks covering two complementary forms of agentic decision making.
ALFWorld ( Shridhar et al., 2021 ) and LOCA-Bench ( Zeng et al., 2026 ) are goal-directed task-execution benchmarks, in which the agent repeatedly acts in the environment to bring the current world into a goal-satisfying state.
RCA-100 ( Cai et al., 2026 ) and ClinDiag ( Chen et al., 2026 ) are evidence-seeking diagnosis benchmarks, where the agent interacts with the environment to acquire discriminative evidence, update competing hypotheses, and ultimately identify the most plausible diagnosis.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text:
We adopt ReAct ( Yao et al., 2023 ) as the common harness for context-management baselines, using its simple reasoning–action loop to keep the interaction protocol consistent while varying the context supplied for action selection. Raw Trajectory directly provides the complete, chronologically ordered action–observation history.
ACON ( Kang et al., 2025 ) and PACE ( Wei et al., 2026 ) manage the growing context through compression and adaptive retention, respectively.
HiAgent ( Hu et al., 2025 ) organizes completed interactions around subgoals and maintains a hierarchical working memory.
LongHorizon-Harness ( Ma et al., 2026 ) maintains an audited task state and coordinates long-horizon execution through a Manage–Execute–Audit architecture.
Together, these baselines cover raw history, compressed and adaptively retained context, hierarchical working memory, and explicitly maintained task state.
LongHorizon-Harness retains its native control architecture, while the remaining baselines operate through the common ReAct harness.

sections.heading: Implementation details.
sections.text:
We evaluate all methods with three backbone models: Qwen3.7-Plus, Kimi-K3, and GLM-5.3. Within each backbone setting, all LLM components of PoS and all LLM-based components of the baselines use the same evaluated backbone.
All LLM calls use deterministic decoding with temperature 0.
Complete benchmark protocols and budgets, baseline implementations, and method-specific hyperparameters are provided in the appendix D .

sections.heading: (1) Existing context management does not consistently improve upon raw trajectories.
sections.text:
Table 1 reveals substantial variation in baseline performance across tasks and backbones.
PACE remains competitive on ALFWorld and RCA-100, but falls 24.57 24.57 – 28.19 28.19 points below Raw Trajectory on LOCA-Bench.
LongHorizon-Harness performs well on LOCA-Bench, where explicit requirements and generated artifacts support intermediate verification, but delivers less consistent gains on RCA-100 and ClinDiag, as progress depends on refining uncertain diagnostic hypotheses rather than producing directly verifiable artifacts.
On ClinDiag with GLM-5.3 , none of the context-management baselines outperforms Raw Trajectory.
These reversals suggest that additional compression and organization do not consistently benefit modern LLMs with strong long-context capabilities, as information loss may offset the benefits of reducing redundancy.

sections.heading: (2) PoS consistently outperforms existing methods across diverse tasks and backbones.
sections.text:
In contrast, PoS achieves the highest overall performance on all four benchmarks under all three backbones.
Compared with the strongest baseline with the same backbone, PoS achieves relative gains of up to 22.68 % 22.68\% on ALFWorld, 7.53 % 7.53\% on LOCA-Bench, 37.89 % 37.89\% on RCA-100 joint accuracy, and 11.31 % 11.31\% on ClinDiag.
The gains span both execution and diagnosis tasks, indicating that they are not tied to a particular task structure.
These results highlight the importance of maintaining an accurate, task-conditioned belief about the current world state and unresolved requirements, beyond retaining and organizing interaction history.

sections.heading: (3) Effective belief modeling requires maintaining both consistency and health.
sections.text:
Removing Consistency Validation lowers performance across all four benchmarks to varying degrees, with losses reaching 14.93 14.93 points on ALFWorld and 11.81 11.81 points on LOCA-Bench, compared with 0.33 0.33 – 0.66 0.66 points on ClinDiag.
This pattern is consistent with the greater risk of inconsistent belief updates when complex interactions require the agent to reconcile changing states and observations across steps.
Removing Trapping Diagnosis and its associated recovery also degrades performance across all four benchmarks, including losses of 4.85 4.85 – 6.79 6.79 points on RCA-100 and 2.65 2.65 – 3.97 3.97 points on ClinDiag.
Recovery complements validation by redirecting actions toward unresolved requirements when continued interaction no longer advances the task.
Together, these results demonstrate the value of maintaining both belief consistency and task progress, beyond constructing an explicit representation.

sections.heading: 4.2 Belief Trapping Analysis
sections.text:
Figure 3 summarizes detected trapping incidence (left), the distribution of trapping patterns (middle), and the effect of recovery strategies after trapping is detected (right).
It reveals that trapping is common across different settings, although stronger backbones generally exhibit lower incidence.
However, lower trapping incidence does not necessarily imply higher final accuracy: on RCA-100, Kimi-K3 exhibits more trapping than GLM-5.3 ( 74 % 74\% vs. 53 % 53\% ) but achieves higher Joint accuracy (Table 1 ).
The dominant trapping pattern also varies across benchmarks, with cycles most frequent in ALFWorld, drift in LOCA-Bench and RCA-100 ( 55.93 % 55.93\% ), and static stagnation in ClinDiag ( 78.25 % 78.25\% ).
These differences reflect how unproductive interactions affect belief transition.
Embodied actions may revisit prior states, multisource evidence may update beliefs without advancing the active gap, and non-discriminative clinical investigations may leave diagnostic beliefs unchanged.
To assess the value of factorized recovery, we compare PoS with a variant that replaces factorized recovery constraints with a generic prompt asking the agent to recover.
Figure 3 (right) shows that PoS ’s recovery strategy outperforms this variant across all four benchmarks.
These results demonstrate that effective recovery goes beyond interrupting unproductive behavior, with factorized recovery tailored to the trapping dynamics and blocked gap type.

sections.heading: 4.3 Cost–Performance Tradeoff
sections.text:
Table 2 examines the cost–performance tradeoff on RCA-100 with Qwen3.7-Plus .
Compared with Raw Trajectory, PoS improves joint accuracy from 24.27 % 24.27\% to 38.83 % 38.83\% , while reducing Task Agent token consumption by 20.9 % 20.9\% .
However, total consumption increases to 5.06 × 5.06\times , as additional computation is devoted to belief construction and maintenance.
Removing Consistency Validation substantially reduces Sentinel overhead and saves 35.6 % 35.6\% of total tokens, but sacrifices 7.76 7.76 points in joint accuracy.
By contrast, removing Trapping Diagnosis and its associated recovery saves only 9.2 % 9.2\% of total tokens, while increasing Task Agent consumption and reducing joint accuracy by 4.85 4.85 points.
Both ablations therefore reduce overall cost but leave the Task Agent consuming more tokens with less accurate final diagnoses.
These results highlight the value of investing additional computation in belief maintenance to improve subsequent decisions, rather than minimizing token consumption alone.

sections.heading: 4.4 Scaling under Context Growth
sections.text:
Figure 4 compares task success on LOCA-Bench as environment descriptions grow from 8K to 256K across three backbones.
Although performance generally declines with context length, ACON shows a more gradual decline than Raw Trajectory at longer contexts.
By compressing accumulated interaction history whenever the context exceeds a predefined threshold, ACON reduces redundancy, whose increasing burden can make compression beneficial despite potential information loss.
Meanwhile, PoS maintains broadly stable performance from 96K to 256K, exceeding the strongest baseline by 10.67 10.67 – 16.00 16.00 points at 256K.
By integrating new observations into an existing world state and unresolved requirements, PoS grounds each decision in the current task conditions rather than requiring the agent to reconstruct them from an increasingly long interaction history.
This incremental maintenance reduces repeated interpretation of dispersed or outdated observations, while consistency validation and progress monitoring help prevent unsupported updates and stalled interactions from persisting.
Together, these results suggest that effective context management should balance reducing historical redundancy with maintaining a reliable and actionable understanding of the current world.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text:
In this work, we showed that explicit belief construction alone is insufficient for reliable long-horizon decision-making.
We proposed PoS , a framework that constructs task-conditioned belief states and continually maintains them through consistency validation and factorized recovery from Belief Trapping .
Experiments across four benchmarks and three LLM backbones demonstrate consistent improvements in execution and diagnosis, together with resilience to context growth.
Although PoS uses more tokens, the resulting gains demonstrate the potential of investing inference-time computation in belief maintenance.
Reducing this overhead while preserving the gains in agent performance is an important direction for future work.

sections.heading: B.1 End-to-End Workflow of PoS
sections.text:
Algorithm 1 summarizes the end-to-end inference workflow of PoS .
It follows the notation introduced in Section 3 and abstracts away implementation-specific details while preserving the main control flow and data dependencies of the framework.
In particular, the Active Gap is maintained across consecutive steps until it is resolved, and trapping is assessed only after the current belief transition has been validated and incorporated into Belief Health.
Any recovery constraint triggered by the resulting health state therefore guides action selection from the subsequent interaction step.

sections.heading: B.2 Belief Trapping Detection and Recovery
Step-level progress assessment.
sections.text:
For diagnostic tasks, c t ​ ( x ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] c_{t}(x)\in[0,1] denotes the confidence assigned to a goal-relevant inferred State or Relation.
These values are maintained independently without normalization across records.
The progress measure in Eq. 4 aggregates absolute confidence changes between consecutive validated beliefs, so both increases and decreases contribute to the progress label when the aggregate change exceeds ϵ \epsilon .
For execution tasks, the Belief Sentinel evaluates progress relative to the active gap using the criteria in Section 3.3 .

sections.heading: Window-based health estimation.
sections.text:
Trapping detection begins once K K validated transitions are available.
At each step t t , historical world states within 𝒲 t \mathcal{W}_{t} are projected onto the same current active gap Δ t \Delta_{t} , selecting relevant records through their existing relations.
The comparison underlying d W d_{W} includes confidence changes even when descriptive content remains unchanged.
When the active gap changes, the existing window is retained and its historical world states are projected onto the new gap.
The resulting persistence, stagnation, and recurrence signals are combined according to Eq. 5 , with trapping detected when ℋ t ≤ θ H \mathcal{H}_{t}\leq\theta_{H} .

sections.heading: Factorized trapping diagnosis.
sections.text:
Once trapping is detected, the Static , Cycle , and Drift conditions are evaluated in order.
If none is satisfied, PoS uses a generic recovery prompt rather than assigning a trapping pattern.
The blocked gap type is selected by comparing persistence across nonempty gap sets.
When persistence is equal, diagnostic tasks prioritize epistemic gaps, whereas execution tasks prioritize achievement gaps.

sections.heading: Recovery constraint composition.
sections.text:
The diagnosed pattern and selected gap type are incorporated into a recovery prompt together with the relevant Entities and the active gap.
The resulting constraints address both the unproductive behavior and the unresolved requirement, and guide subsequent action selection while the active gap remains unchanged.
After each validated transition, PoS recomputes belief health and releases the constraints when ℋ t > θ H \mathcal{H}_{t}>\theta_{H} .
Otherwise, it updates the diagnosis and corresponding recovery constraints.

sections.heading: B.3 Design Rationale for Belief Trapping
Choice of trapping signals.
sections.text:
The three signals capture complementary aspects of unproductive interaction.
Gap Persistence ties the assessment to requirements that remain unresolved, while Progress Stagnation measures the absence of recorded task progress.
Belief Recurrence complements these signals by identifying repeated belief configurations that may occur despite positive step-level progress labels.
Behavioral statistics such as action repetition or interaction count do not directly establish whether the task is advancing.
Repeated tool calls may acquire relevant information, whereas different actions may leave the same requirement unresolved.
Likewise, confidence levels alone do not indicate progress, as high confidence can persist during stalled investigation and low confidence can accompany useful evidence gathering.
The selected signals instead connect unresolved requirements with changes and recurring patterns in the maintained belief.

sections.heading: Aggregation of trapping signals.
sections.text:
We design the health score to capture stagnation or recurrence associated with persistent unresolved requirements, without treating gap persistence alone as sufficient evidence of trapping.
Let p t = max X ∈ { E , A } ⁡ P X p_{t}=\max_{X\in\{E,A\}}P_{X} denote the largest gap persistence within the current window.
A geometric mean can miss trapping because stagnation and recurrence need not occur together.
Specifically, ℋ t geo = 1 − ( p t ​ S t ​ R t ) 1 / 3 \mathcal{H}_{t}^{\mathrm{geo}}=1-(p_{t}S_{t}R_{t})^{1/3} yields ℋ t geo = 1 \mathcal{H}_{t}^{\mathrm{geo}}=1 whenever either S t S_{t} or R t R_{t} is zero, regardless of how high the other signals are.
An agent may make no progress without revisiting earlier beliefs, or repeatedly return to earlier beliefs while confidence changes produce positive progress labels.
In either case, the absence of one signal prevents the geometric mean from identifying trapping.
By contrast, ℋ t max = 1 − max ⁡ ( p t , S t , R t ) \mathcal{H}_{t}^{\mathrm{max}}=1-\max(p_{t},S_{t},R_{t}) can incorrectly identify trapping solely because unresolved requirements persist.
When p t = 1 p_{t}=1 , it yields ℋ t max = 0 \mathcal{H}_{t}^{\mathrm{max}}=0 even if S t = R t = 0 S_{t}=R_{t}=0 , meaning that every transition records progress and no belief recurrence is detected.
A gap may remain unresolved throughout the window while the agent makes intermediate progress toward resolving it.
The maximum formulation therefore confuses an unfinished requirement with stalled progress. PoS therefore uses ℋ t = 1 − p t ​ max ⁡ ( S t , R t ) , \mathcal{H}_{t}=1-p_{t}\max(S_{t},R_{t}), (8) which weights the stronger stagnation or recurrence signal by the persistence of unresolved requirements.
This preserves sensitivity to either form of unproductive belief evolution without treating gap persistence alone as sufficient evidence of trapping.

sections.heading: Appendix D Implementation and Reproducibility Details
D.1 Backbone and Agent Configuration
sections.text:
We evaluate all methods with three backbone models: Qwen3.7-Plus , Kimi-K3 , and GLM-5.3 .
The model is accessed through the DashScope OpenAI-compatible API ( https://dashscope.aliyuncs.com/compatible-mode/v1 ); no fixed API snapshot is available.
For each backbone setting, all LLM-based components of PoS and baselines use the same backbone as the corresponding baseline agents.
We do not use a stronger auxiliary model for belief construction, validation, or trapping-aware recovery.
The Task Agent selects its action from the current task-conditioned belief state, which serves as its decision context.
The only model fixed independently of the evaluated backbone occurs in the medical diagnosis benchmark ClinDiag.
Its provider and judge are treated as part of the benchmark environment rather than as components of the evaluated agent.
To keep this environment identical across backbone settings, both are implemented with Qwen3.7-plus for all methods and backbones.
All agent-side model calls use deterministic decoding with temperature 0 0 .
We set the maximum generation length to 512 tokens for ALFWorld, where each interaction primarily requires selecting an environment action, and to 4096 tokens for LOCA-Bench, RCA-100, and ClinDiag.

sections.heading: D.2 Baseline Selection
sections.text:
We select baselines to cover representative forms of decision context while remaining applicable under a common cross-domain evaluation setting.
Raw Trajectory serves as the uncompressed reference and exposes the complete interaction history directly to the Agent.
Among memory-based approaches, ACON [ Kang et al., 2025 ] , PACE [ Wei et al., 2026 ] , and HiAgent [ Hu et al., 2025 ] represent complementary strategies based on history compression, adaptive context granularity, and hierarchical subgoal-oriented working memory, respectively.
We further include LongHorizon-Harness [ Ma et al., 2026 ] as a closely related state-oriented baseline because it explicitly maintains an audited task state across long-horizon execution.
Together, these methods span raw history, compressed and selectively retained context, hierarchical memory, and explicit task-state maintenance, while remaining adaptable to the same four evaluation environments and backbone settings.
We do not attempt to exhaustively benchmark every method discussed in Section 2 , as several approaches differ substantially in their training assumptions, control architecture, or task-specific state representation.
For example, SUPO [ Lu et al., 2026 ] jointly optimizes summarization and tool-use policies through reinforcement learning, while CaT [ Liu et al., 2026 ] and AgentFold [ Ye et al., 2026 ] rely on learned policies for actively manipulating the working context.
Several belief-oriented methods are likewise specialized to particular reasoning structures or task families.
In particular, Graph of States [ Luo et al., 2026 ] is designed for abductive reasoning and couples belief representation with a causal graph and a state machine that explicitly constrain hypothesis evolution, making its representation closely tied to diagnosis-style tasks rather than a common decision context that can be applied unchanged across all four benchmarks.
Similarly, Tru-POMDP [ Tang et al., 2026 ] assumes structured hypotheses and belief-space planning for uncertain task planning.
We therefore prioritize baselines that provide representative and practically comparable alternatives to PoS under a unified cross-domain evaluation protocol.

sections.heading: Shared evaluation protocol.
sections.text:
We evaluate all baselines through the same benchmark adapters, tool
interfaces, task instructions, termination protocol, and environment-action
budgets described in Appendix C .
All LLM-based components follow the backbone configuration described in
Appendix D.1 .
Because different policies naturally induce different interaction
trajectories, the methods do not receive identical observations; instead,
they share the same evidence-acquisition interface and differ in how the
evidence produced by their own interactions is represented and exposed for
subsequent decision making.
Raw Trajectory, ACON, PACE, and HiAgent are integrated into a common
ReAct harness [ Yao et al., 2023 ] .
LongHorizon-Harness retains its native Manage–Execute–Audit control
structure, while using the same benchmark adapters, tools, backbone, and
environment-action budget.

sections.heading: Material implementation differences.
sections.text:
The original baselines were developed for different environments and agent
protocols, so their end-to-end runners cannot be directly applied to all four
benchmarks.
We preserve the defining context-management mechanism of each method while
adapting its interaction layer to the common benchmark interfaces.
All methods receive the same task-independent background information, tool
documentation, and termination instructions.
Method-specific prompts contain only the instructions required to construct
or operate the corresponding context representation.
When an original response format is incompatible with the benchmark tool
interface, we provide format demonstrations containing only interface-level
examples and no evaluated cases or target answers.

sections.heading: ACON.
sections.text:
ACON learns compression guidelines from contrasting successful and failed
trajectories and can further distill the optimized compressor [ Kang et al., 2025 ] .
Our evaluation benchmarks do not provide dedicated training splits for
learning such benchmark-specific compression policies, while optimizing them
on evaluation cases would conflate inference-time context management with
task-specific training.
We therefore preserve ACON’s runtime history-compression mechanism but use
fixed benchmark-level preservation guidelines without failure-driven
guideline optimization or compressor distillation.
The guidelines are case-independent and specify only generic categories of
information that should be retained.
Compression thresholds and output budgets are fixed at the benchmark level
and shared across all evaluated backbones.

sections.heading: PACE.
sections.text:
PACE retains the interaction history in an external chunk store and exposes
each chunk at an adaptive granularity determined by its predicted relevance
to the next decision [ Wei et al., 2026 ] .
We preserve its four representation levels, relevance-based granularity
selection, chronological ordering, and glimpse mechanism.
Because the repository linked by the paper was inaccessible during our
implementation, we reproduce the method from its published equations,
default settings, and Algorithm 1.
The original BGE-M3 encoder is replaced with text-embedding-v4 for relevance scoring, while the evaluated
backbone generates the textual detailed and brief representations.

sections.heading: HiAgent.
sections.text:
HiAgent organizes working memory around Agent-generated subgoals [ Hu et al., 2025 ] .
The trajectory associated with the active subgoal is retained in full,
whereas completed subgoals are represented by summaries and their original
trajectories remain available for retrieval.
Since the official implementation is built on AgentBoard, we port the
subgoal-based working-memory mechanism into the shared benchmark interface
and convert its interaction protocol to the common structured action format.
Summary-length and folding parameters are adapted at the benchmark level and
then fixed across all cases and backbone models.

sections.heading: LongHorizon-Harness.
sections.text:
LongHorizon-Harness differs from the other baselines in that it defines a complete Manage–Execute–Audit control architecture rather than only a context representation [ Ma et al., 2026 ] .
At each round, the Manager constructs a bounded subtask from the audited task state, the Executor interacts with the environment to complete it, and the Auditor verifies the resulting state before verified requirements, artifacts, and facts are propagated to the next round.
We base our implementation on the official LongHorizon-Harness codebase and preserve its native Manager–Executor–Auditor workflow and audited task-state
representation.
We only adapt the benchmark-facing tool interfaces and action formats so that the method can operate through the same evaluation interfaces as the other baselines.
Any Auditor operation that queries the environment is counted against the same environment-action budget as an Executor action; purely internal Manager, Executor, or Auditor LLM calls are treated as computational overhead.

sections.heading: D.4 PoS Hyperparameters
sections.text:
Table 8 summarizes the hyperparameter configuration of PoS .
Belief updates and local consistency audits are scheduled at every interaction step, while global audits are scheduled every 32 steps on LOCA-Bench and every 8 steps on the other benchmarks.
The diagnostic progress threshold applies to RCA-100 and ClinDiag, whereas execution progress is assessed by the Belief Sentinel.

sections.heading: Appendix E Fine-Grained Main Results
sections.text:
Table 9 expands the aggregate results in Table 1 into task categories and diagnostic dimensions.
This breakdown reveals which task requirements benefit from explicit belief maintenance, how validation and recovery contribute to different aspects of performance, and where challenges remain.

sections.heading: (1) Explicit belief particularly benefits state tracking and diagnostic disambiguation.
sections.text:
A key benefit of explicit belief is that observations from different steps jointly inform an updated understanding of the current world.
By maintaining this understanding together with unresolved gaps, PoS connects what the agent has already established to what its next action must accomplish.
This is particularly useful when successful execution depends on preserving state changes across actions, or when diagnosis requires combining several signals to distinguish competing hypotheses.
The concentration of ALFWorld gains in Transform supports this interpretation, with Qwen3.7-Plus success increasing from 56.00 % 56.00\% to 81.33 % 81.33\% , while Place matches the strongest baseline at 97.56 % 97.56\% .
Our RCA-100 trace analysis further shows how belief integrates “request patterns” and “resource-utilization” signals around an identified entity, allowing the agent to rule out failure types that conflict with the accumulated observations.
Most failure-type corrections occur in cases where Raw Trajectory already identifies the correct entity but misclassifies its failure, including 14 cases with Kimi-K3 and 16 with GLM-5.3 .
Together with the trace analysis, this highlights how explicit belief consolidates failure characteristics around an entity, while the Active Gap directs further investigation toward evidence that distinguishes competing hypotheses.

sections.heading: (2) Validation and recovery support different aspects of diagnostic performance.
sections.text:
On RCA-100, removing Consistency Validation reduces RCL by only 0.97 0.97 points under each backbone, but lowers FT by 6.80 6.80 points with Qwen3.7-Plus.
This contrast highlights the importance of validating inferred fault states even when the agent can still locate the incident.
Removing Trapping Diagnosis and its associated recovery has a larger effect on localization, reducing RCL by 3.88 3.88 – 4.85 4.85 points.
The distinction also appears in ClinDiag’s Rare subset, where removing validation lowers accuracy by 0.33 0.33 points under each backbone, whereas removing recovery causes losses of 2.31 2.31 – 3.64 3.64 points.
These results show that the two mechanisms address different needs within diagnosis.
Validation checks whether belief updates remain consistent and supported, while recovery redirects investigation when the current course of interaction no longer resolves diagnostic uncertainty.

sections.heading: (3) Better decision context does not replace execution skills or domain knowledge.
sections.text:
Explicit belief construction and maintenance improve how task information is represented and updated, but successful completion also depends on the model’s ability to act on that information.
Although PoS achieves the highest success on LOCA-Bench’s Env.Ops category under every backbone, performance remains between 36.00 % 36.00\% and 41.14 % 41.14\% .
These tasks also demand reliable tool use and action sequencing, as identifying the required state change is different from executing the operations that produce it.
Our ClinDiag trace analysis reveals a related limitation, with many incorrect diagnoses arising after the agent receives correct information but lacks the medical knowledge needed to interpret it.
Even an accurate representation of the current World State is insufficient when the agent lacks the execution skills or domain knowledge required to complete the task.
Addressing these limitations requires improvements in tool-use competence and domain-specific reasoning alongside belief maintenance, rather than relying on context management alone.

sections.heading: Appendix G Limitations and Future Directions
sections.text: Two limitations motivate future work on the efficiency of belief maintenance and the reliability of knowledge-dependent reasoning in PoS.

sections.heading: (1) Cost of explicit belief maintenance.
sections.text:
The performance gains of PoS come with additional token and computational costs.
Its natural language form structured Belief States require repeated text processing and generation during maintenance and subsequent reasoning.
Repeatedly expressing and revising beliefs in language introduces redundancy and may cause information omission or semantic distortion.
Future work could explore task-conditioned latent world-state representations that encode decision-relevant information more compactly and support incremental updates without repeatedly expanding the state into text.
The key is to encode information about the current world state in a latent representation with high information density that can be efficiently propagated and updated within the model.
We aim to preserve an accurate understanding of the current world state while substantially reducing the token and computational costs of belief maintenance.

sections.heading: (2) Dependence on domain and task knowledge.
sections.text:
Although PoS receives external observations through tools, it does not systematically integrate external domain-knowledge retrieval into belief construction and reasoning.
Its ability to identify relevant evidence and interpret observations therefore depends largely on the backbone model’s existing knowledge.
Insufficient knowledge may lead to omitted facts or incorrect causal and diagnostic judgments, even when the resulting Belief State is internally consistent.
Future work could incorporate domain-knowledge retrieval into belief updates and evidence interpretation, helping the agent determine what information to retain and how it supports or contradicts competing explanations.
By incorporating relevant domain knowledge, we aim to improve the accuracy of Belief States and the reliability of subsequent reasoning in specialized tasks.

Abstract
Large language model (LLM) agents can now undertake increasingly complex tasks, but the way they organize interaction history into memory does not ensure a coherent understanding of the current world.
We introduce
PoS
, an inference-time framework that constructs and continually maintains explicit belief states as the agent’s decision context.
Each belief combines an estimate of the current world state with unresolved task requirements, making explicit what the agent still needs to learn and accomplish.
To keep this belief reliable and actionable,
PoS
validates its consistency and monitors task progress to detect
Belief Trapping
, where the agent continues to act without making meaningful progress toward the goal.
Recovery is then tailored to both the trapping pattern and the type of unresolved task requirement.
Experiments on four benchmarks spanning execution and diagnosis show that
PoS
achieves the highest overall performance on every benchmark with all three LLM backbones.
Ablations demonstrate the importance of consistency validation and recovery, while context-scaling experiments show resilience to context growth.
Together, these results support belief construction and continual maintenance as a foundation for long-horizon context management beyond history retention and compression.

Introduction
LLM agents are increasingly equipped with ultra-long context windows
(
Yang et al., 2025
;
Xu et al., 2026a
;
Hu et al., 2026
)
, stronger reasoning and tool-use capabilities
(
Guo et al., 2025
;
Feng et al., 2026
)
, external memory systems
(
Hu et al., 2025
;
Kang et al., 2025
;
Wei et al., 2026
;
Xu et al., 2026b
)
, and sophisticated execution harnesses
(
Ma et al., 2026
;
Wan et al., 2026
)
, substantially expanding the complexity and horizon of tasks they can undertake.
However, longer interaction horizons expose a deeper challenge, as actions may alter the environment and new observations may invalidate earlier inferences.
Accumulated context thus mixes evidence about past states with intermediate judgments, making it increasingly difficult to identify which facts still hold, which inferences remain supported, and what remains unresolved.
Raw trajectories preserve this evidence chronologically, while memory mechanisms select, compress, or reorganize it.
While both are valuable, access to evidence alone does not ensure an explicit and coherent estimate of the current world that can be revised and checked across steps.
Recent work observes that when task state remains implicit within a growing context, outdated or inconsistent information can persist across subsequent decisions
(
Ma et al., 2026
)
.
The next barrier to reliable long-horizon LLM agents is therefore not simply retaining more history, but maintaining an actionable representation of the current world.

In a standard partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), this belief is a sufficient statistic for decision-making and can be recursively updated after each action and observation

Recent methods have begun to explicitly represent the belief state through goal-relative reflection, probabilistic hypotheses, structured graphs, or audited task records

Such representations make the agent’s current understanding of the world available for inspection and revision.
However, explicit belief construction is just the start, as an LLM-generated belief must satisfy two further requirements.
First, belief updates must remain internally consistent and supported by interaction evidence.
Since these updates are generated by the LLM itself, they may introduce conflicting states or unsupported inferences that undermine subsequent decisions and ultimately lead to task failure.
For instance, recording a microwave as both open and closed makes it unclear whether the robot should open it before placing a mug inside.
Continual validation is thus essential to sustain the coherence and evidential support of the evolving belief state.
Second, consistency alone does not prevent the failure mode we term
Belief Trapping
, where the agent continues to act without making meaningful progress toward the goal.
For example, the agent may repeat ineffective actions, cycle through previously visited states, or gather information that does not help complete the task.
Unproductive interactions will exhaust the available budget before achieving the goal, making timely detection and recovery necessary to restore meaningful task progress.

2
Related Work
We organize prior approaches to long-horizon context management according to the decision context they expose to the agent:
memory as context
and
belief as context
.
2.1
Memory as Context
ReAct
(
Yao et al., 2023
)
provides a foundational framework for LLM agents, conditioning each action on the growing raw interaction trajectory.
Compression-based methods instead summarize accumulated context into compact forms: ReadAgent
(
Lee et al., 2024
)
constructs retrievable gist memories, ACON
(
Kang et al., 2025
)
optimizes guidelines for history compression, and SUPO
(
Lu et al., 2026
)
jointly learns periodic summarization and tool-use policies.
Other methods impose structure on the retained context: HiAgent
(
Hu et al., 2025
)
organizes working memory around subgoals, COMPASS
(
Wan et al., 2026
)
maintains concise progress briefs across reasoning stages, and PACE
(
Wei et al., 2026
)
adjusts historical granularity according to its predicted relevance to the next action.
Other approaches make context management itself an agent-controlled operation: MemGPT manages information across in-context and external memory through an operating-system-inspired hierarchy
(
Packer et al., 2023
)
. CaT
(
Liu et al., 2026
)
exposes context compression as a callable tool over a structured workspace, AgentFold
(
Ye et al., 2026
)
performs proactive multi-scale folding of historical trajectories, and Sculptor
(
Li et al., 2026
)
provides explicit tools for actively curating the working context.
Although these methods improve evidence accessibility and context efficiency, the resulting context remains a transformed record of historical evidence rather than a consistent estimate of the current world.
2.2
Belief as Context
A parallel line of work studies how LLMs represent the current state of an evolving world
(
Gurnee and Tegmark, 2024
)
.
Mechanistic studies probe the world-state abstractions encoded by LLMs
(
Li et al., 2024
)
and show that state tracking of reasoning is itself a learned computation whose underlying mechanism affects systematic generalization
(
Li et al., 2025
)
.
Agent frameworks further externalize parts of this computation
(
Tang et al., 2024
)
.
QuBE
(
Kim et al., 2024
)
constructs a task-relevant belief through question answering; StateAct
(
Rozanov and Rei, 2025
)
maintains a chain of states throughout task execution; and ReflAct
(
Kim et al., 2025
)
grounds action selection in reflection over the current state relative to the goal.
More structured approaches maintain particle beliefs over latent states and goals through hypothesis trees and Bayesian filtering
(
Tang et al., 2026
)
, recursively update natural-language belief summaries
(
Lidayan et al., 2025
)
, or combine causal graphs with state machines as explicit belief
(
Luo et al., 2026
)
.
LongHorizon-Harness
(
Ma et al., 2026
)
externalizes task state as audited records of requirements, artifacts, and facts, preserving verified progress through a Manage-Execute-Audit loop.
However, it relies on independently verifiable intermediate results and is therefore less suitable when meaningful progress consists of uncertain inferences rather than observable outcomes.
Beyond belief construction, recent work has also begun to address failure modes related to
Belief Trapping
.
T
3
(
Zou et al., 2026
)
detects excessive belief deviation and truncates uninformative trajectories during reinforcement learning, while CGDP
(
Kausik et al., 2026
)
uses an exhaustion gate to terminate unproductive context gathering.
These approaches address stalled progress through truncation or termination, without attempting to restore progress during inference.
In contrast,
PoS
maintains and validates a task-conditioned belief and uses factorized recovery to redirect subsequent actions.

We evaluate

ALFWorld
(
Shridhar et al., 2021

and LOCA-Bench

RCA-100
(
Cai et al., 2026
)
and ClinDiag
(
Chen et al., 2026
)
are
evidence-seeking diagnosis
benchmarks, where the agent interacts with the environment to acquire discriminative evidence, update competing hypotheses, and ultimately identify the most plausible diagnosis.
Baselines.
We adopt ReAct
(
Yao et al., 2023
)
as the common harness for context-management baselines, using its simple reasoning–action loop to keep the interaction protocol consistent while varying the context supplied for action selection.
Raw Trajectory
directly provides the complete, chronologically ordered action–observation history.
ACON
(
Kang et al., 2025
)
and PACE
(
Wei et al., 2026
)
manage the growing context through compression and adaptive retention, respectively.
HiAgent
(
Hu et al., 2025
)
organizes completed interactions around subgoals and maintains a hierarchical working memory.
LongHorizon-Harness
(
Ma et al., 2026
)
maintains an audited task state and coordinates long-horizon execution through a Manage–Execute–Audit architecture.
Together, these baselines cover raw history, compressed and adaptively retained context, hierarchical working memory, and explicitly maintained task state.
LongHorizon-Harness retains its native control architecture, while the remaining baselines operate through the common ReAct harness.

We evaluate all methods with three backbone models:

Within each backbone setting, all LLM components of
PoS
and all LLM-based components of the baselines use the same evaluated backbone.

5
Conclusion
In this work, we showed that explicit belief construction alone is insufficient for reliable long-horizon decision-making.
We proposed
PoS
, a framework that constructs task-conditioned belief states and continually maintains them through consistency validation and factorized recovery from
Belief Trapping
.
Experiments across four benchmarks and three LLM backbones demonstrate consistent improvements in execution and diagnosis, together with resilience to context growth.
Although
PoS
uses more tokens, the resulting gains demonstrate the potential of investing inference-time computation in belief maintenance.
Reducing this overhead while preserving the gains in agent performance is an important direction for future work.

B.3
Design Rationale for Belief Trapping
Choice of trapping signals.
The three signals capture complementary aspects of unproductive interaction.
Gap Persistence ties the assessment to requirements that remain unresolved, while Progress Stagnation measures the absence of recorded task progress.
Belief Recurrence complements these signals by identifying repeated belief configurations that may occur despite positive step-level progress labels.
Behavioral statistics such as action repetition or interaction count do not directly establish whether the task is advancing.
Repeated tool calls may acquire relevant information, whereas different actions may leave the same requirement unresolved.
Likewise, confidence levels alone do not indicate progress, as high confidence can persist during stalled investigation and low confidence can accompany useful evidence gathering.
The selected signals instead connect unresolved requirements with changes and recurring patterns in the maintained belief.

C.3
Interactive Evaluation Protocols
All methods interact with each benchmark through the same benchmark-specific interface.
The context-management baselines operate within the shared ReAct harness, while LongHorizon-Harness retains its native Manage–Execute–Audit control structure.
•
ALFWorld.
The agent receives a natural-language goal and an initial textual observation.
At each step, it executes one command from the environment’s admissible action set and receives the resulting observation.
A case succeeds when the environment confirms that the goal conditions have been satisfied; otherwise, it terminates when the action budget is exhausted.
•
LOCA-Bench.
The agent receives a task instruction and a case-specific set of MCP tools for inspecting and modifying the task environment.
Each tool call constitutes one environment action, and its result becomes the next observation.
The agent invokes the
‘‘claim_done’’
tool after completing the task, after which the official evaluator determines success; an uncompleted case terminates upon budget exhaustion.
•
RCA-100.
The agent initially receives the incident metadata, while metrics, logs, traces, events, alerts, and system topology must be acquired through diagnostic tools.
Each tool call constitutes one environment action.
The agent terminates the case by calling
‘‘submit_root_cause’’
with a fault type and a root-cause entity.
We evaluate the two submitted fields separately and report joint accuracy when both are correct; cases without a valid submission before the action budget are treated as failures.
•
ClinDiag.
The agent initially observes only the patient’s initial presentation.
It acquires additional evidence by asking one specific question per action about medical history, physical examination, laboratory tests, radiographic tests, or other diagnostic procedures.
The case terminates when the agent calls
‘‘submit_diagnosis’’
, and the submitted diagnosis is evaluated against the reference diagnosis by the benchmark judge.
Cases without a valid submission before the action budget are treated as failures.

We select baselines to cover representative forms of decision context while remaining applicable under a common cross-domain evaluation setting.
Raw Trajectory serves as the uncompressed reference and exposes the complete interaction history directly to the Agent.
Among memory-based approaches, ACON

Appendix G
Limitations and Future Directions
Two limitations motivate future work on the efficiency of belief maintenance and the reliability of knowledge-dependent reasoning in PoS.
(1) Cost of explicit belief maintenance.
The performance gains of
PoS
come with additional token and computational costs.
Its natural language form structured Belief States require repeated text processing and generation during maintenance and subsequent reasoning.
Repeatedly expressing and revising beliefs in language introduces redundancy and may cause information omission or semantic distortion.
Future work could explore task-conditioned
latent world-state representations
that encode decision-relevant information more compactly and support incremental updates without repeatedly expanding the state into text.
The key is to encode information about the current world state in a latent representation with high information density that can be efficiently propagated and updated within the model.
We aim to preserve an accurate understanding of the current world state while substantially reducing the token and computational costs of belief maintenance.
(2) Dependence on domain and task knowledge.
Although
PoS
receives external observations through tools, it does not systematically integrate external domain-knowledge retrieval into belief construction and reasoning.
Its ability to identify relevant evidence and interpret observations therefore depends largely on the backbone model’s existing knowledge.
Insufficient knowledge may lead to omitted facts or incorrect causal and diagnostic judgments, even when the resulting Belief State is internally consistent.
Future work could incorporate
domain-knowledge retrieval
into belief updates and evidence interpretation, helping the agent determine what information to retain and how it supports or contradicts competing explanations.
By incorporating relevant domain knowledge, we aim to improve the accuracy of Belief States and the reliability of subsequent reasoning in specialized tasks.
